newsitem.title: USA: Some tobacco negotiators optimistic deal is near.
newsitem.headline: Some tobacco negotiators optimistic deal is near.

text.p: Negotiators for states and the tobacco industry desperately tried to resolve contentious issues on Thursday and reach a landmark tobacco settlement of lawsuits by the end of the week.
"We're very optimistic. We hope to present (Thursday) an agreement in principle to the White House," Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger told Boston's WBZ-AM radio.

Talks between tobacco industry representatives and the state attorneys general have been going on since early April. The negotiations are aimed at a broad settlement of the huge legal claims against the industry in return for some form of increased regulation and curbs on advertising and marketing of tobacco products.

Forty states have sued the industry to recoup the costs of treating sick smokers. The states are demanding that the industry agree to be punished for past actions, that it pay compensatory and punitive damages for smoking-related injuries and that it agree to allow the Food and Drug Administration to regulate cigarettes as a drug.
Sources close to both the state attorneys general and the tobacco industry said they doubted a deal would be reached until late Thursday at the soonest, and some said they thought it might be Friday.
Asked how talks were progressing, Richard Scruggs, a Mississippi lawyer assisting several of the states, replied, "The horse is still breathing."
The main negotiator representing the anti-smoking, American health organisations, Matthew Myers, was absent Thursday to attend a funeral.
Connecticut Attorney General Richard Blumenthal said two areas of disagreement remained.

"One, details as to the terms of any final settlement protecting public health," Blumenthal said. "And the larger issues relating to assuring that people's rights are protected to sue the industry for the harm that's done," he told WTIC-AM radio in Hartford, Conn.
Major tobacco companies Philip Morris Cos. Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., and Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. declined to comment on the negotiations.
The White House has taken a keen interest in the talks but has been careful not to appear to be running them.

Negotiators have considered turning over an incomplete proposal to the White House and asking it to resolve the contentious issue of whether the industry would pay so-called punitive damages, according to sources close to the talks. Punitive damages are awarded to punish and deter wrongful behaviour.

In an interview with the Wall Street Journal published Thursday, President Bill Clinton urged tobacco companies and anti-smoking forces to stay at the negotiating table until they reached an agreement. However, he did not preclude personally intervening if he is convinced the two sides have exhausted all hope of reaching a deal.

"I don't want to rule in or out what I might say, but I want these parties to come to me and say, 'This is where we are. We've done all we can do, here's where we are,'" Clinton said in an interview conducted on Wednesday. "And I want them to do the very best they can first."

Clinton left Washington on Thursday for a summit of world leaders in Denver without his top adviser on the tobacco negotiations, Bruce Lindsey, who stayed behind to monitor the talks. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Lindsey would delay his departure for Denver until Saturday.

The states want to wind up the talks this week. If there is no agreement, Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore has said he will go ahead with presenting a case against the industry at the first trial of a state suit set for July 7.
